cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: A crime requires two elements: actus reus (the guilty act) and mens rea (the guilty mind)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Actus reus can be a positive act, a failure to act (omission) or a state of affairs

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Omissions generally do not create criminal liability unless there is a duty to act (e.g. parent–child, contract)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Causation requires both factual causation ('but for' test) and legal causation (proximate cause)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Legal causation can be broken by a novus actus interveniens (new intervening act)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Mens rea is the mental element of a crime — it varies between offences

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Intention is the highest form of mens rea — direct intent (aim) or oblique intent (foreseen consequence)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Recklessness is taking an unjustifiable risk — the defendant was aware of the risk but took it anyway

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Strict liability offences require only actus reus — no mens rea is needed (e.g. speeding, selling alcohol to minors)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Transferred malice applies when a defendant intends to harm one person but accidentally harms another

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: The defendant must be sufficiently voluntary in their actions — automatism negates actus reus

cards.front: Recall a key point about Elements of Crime
cards.back: Both actus reus and mens rea must coincide at the same time for most crimes
